newsitem.title: USA: CBOT/EPA sell 300,000 emission permits for $32 mln.
newsitem.headline: CBOT/EPA sell 300,000 emission permits for $32 mln.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Wednesday they sold 300,000 pollution allowances for a total of $32.2 million during their fifth annual sulfur dioxide emissions auction.
The March 24 auction was divided into three tranches, with sale of 150,000 spot allowances usable this year producing an average winning bid of $110.36, up from $68.14 last year.
"We are very pleased that in this fifth year, things are going quite strong," said Brian McLean, EPA acid rain division director, via telephone during a joint conference here.

Emission permits sold through the CBOT auction comprise only 2.8 percent of all available allowances traded in the United States under a program created by the 1990 Clean Air Act to reduce air pollution, the EPA said.
Each transferable permit allows its holder, such as a utility, to release up to one ton of sulfur dioxide, a major component of "acid" rain, into the air.

The CBOT has regulatory permission to open a futures contract based on sulfur dioxide emissions but has chosen not to launch it because the market is not developed enough, said Patrick Videll in CBOT's marketing department.
CBOT said Monday's auction for the first time produced a winning bidder from outside the United States, among special interest groups that buy and retire the air pollution permits.
The St John's Ecology Club in Guam paid $1,022.49 for nine allowances, according to 1997 auction results.

CBOT said this year that six elementary or middle schools (including St John's), three universities, and six public interest groups won allowances during the auction. Last year, 19 different special interest groups won allowances.
Special interest groups bought less then two percent of 1997 allowances. Utilities and brokerages bought the majority.
